MEX$170 billion between 2018 and 2021","locator":"page 90","attribution":"Mexican authorities (as cited in IMF Article IV Consultation Report)","period_fit":"2018-2021","source_limitations":["VAT gap reduction estimate is based on authorities' own analysis rather than independent audit","Other concurrent reforms and shocks may have contributed to compliance improvement"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 90. to adaptation of non-compliance behavior and, possibly, a smaller base of evasion and
avoidance from which additional revenues can be obtained","locator":"page 90","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"Medium-term outlook as of 2022","source_limitations":["Analytical assessment rather than quantified projection","Border compliance overlap with security issues adds uncertainty"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 90. The candidate adds 'border security-tax administration overlap' from the following sentence in the source; this is consistent with the source's discussion but extends beyond the extracted excerpt. Attribution and polarity are correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0163","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The means-tested social pension was replaced by a basic pension starting in 2019, with increases in contribution rates, adjustments to minimum pensions, and changes to minimum contribution requirements following in 2021.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government","action":"reformed pension system","mechanism":["replacement of means-tested social pension with basic pension","contribution rate increases","minimum pension adjustments","minimum contribution requirement changes"],"outcome":"Radical changes to the 1997 pension system vision, which was never fully operational due to lengthy transition period","dates":["2019","2021"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Starting in 2019,
the means-tested social pension was replaced by a basic pension with increases in contribution rates
and adjustments to minimum pensions and minimum contribution requirements following in 2021","locator":"page 91","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"2019-2021 reforms","source_limitations":["Reforms are described as radical but long-term effects uncertain","Transition from 1997 system which was never fully operational complicates baseline assessment"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 91. Dates, mechanism elements, and attribution are consistent with source."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0164","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Contribution rates to the mandatory defined contributory system will increase from 6.5-10 percent to 15 percent by 2030, with employer contributions rising to 13.875 percent for high earners while lower earners will be subsidized by the government.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government","action":"increased pension contribution rates","mechanism":["phased increase in employer contribution rates","government subsidy for low earners"],"outcome":"Contribution rates rising from 6.5-10% to 15% by 2030; government contributions changing from 2023; employer rates reaching final values in 2030","dates":["2023","2030"],"quantities":["6.5 percent","10 percent","15 percent","13.875 percent"],"excerpt":"An increase in contribution rates from 6.5–10 percent to 15 percent by 2030. Currently,
employees pay 1.125 percent of earnings, the government 0.225 percent (plus a social quota
depending on earnings), and the employer 5.15 percent. This leads to a range of contribution
rates from 6.5 percent for high earners to 10 percent for low earners. Total contributions are set
to rise to 15 percent by increasing employer contributions to 13.875 percent for high earners,
while lower earners will be subsidized by the government","locator":"page 91","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"2020-2030 reform implementation period","source_limitations":["Contribution rate increases phased over ten years; final values not reached until 2030","Government subsidy structure for low earners adds complexity to distributional assessment"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 91. Quantities (6.5%, 10%, 15%, 13.875%) and dates (2023, 2030) match source. Attribution is correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0165","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The minimum years of contributions required to receive an earnings-related pension was reduced from approximately 25 years to 15 years in 2021, with yearly increases planned so that a minimum of 20 years is reached by 2031.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government","action":"reduced minimum pension contribution years","mechanism":["legislative reform lowering qualifying period","phased increase in minimum years"],"outcome":"Near-term eligibility improved; minimum of 20 years required by 2031; some pensioners became immediately eligible in 2021 who would not have been under previous 25-year rule","dates":["2021","2031"],"quantities":["15 years","20 years","25 years"],"excerpt":"The 2021 reforms lowered this to 15 years in 2021 but provide for yearly
increases so that a minimum of 20 years is reached by 2031","locator":"page 91","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"2021 reform; phased increase through 2031","source_limitations":["Phased increase means minimum qualifying period will rise again over time","Those close to retirement under post-1997 system benefited most; long-term workers face higher eventual thresholds"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 91. The claim's 'approximately 25 years' for the prior requirement is supported by the source text which states 'close to 25 years' as the pre-2021 minimum. Quantities (15 years, 20 years) and dates (2021, 2031) match source."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0166","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"From 2022, caps on fees charged by AFOREs (pension fund administrators) cannot exceed average fees in Chile, Colombia, and the United States.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government","action":"capped AFORE fees","mechanism":["fee cap set relative to international benchmark average"],"outcome":"Fee cap on AFORE charges established at average of Chile, Colombia, and US fee levels","dates":["2022"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Caps on fees charged by AFOREs. From 2022, fees cannot exceed average fees in Chile,
Colombia, and the U.S","locator":"page 92","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"2022","source_limitations":["Cap is set relative to other countries' average fees rather than an absolute cost standard","Whether this represents a meaningful reduction from prior Mexican fees is not stated"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 92. Date (2022) and mechanism (fee cap relative to international average) match source. Attribution is correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0167","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Government spending on pensions increased from 1.4 percent of GDP in 2000 to 4.0 percent of GDP in 2021, representing a near-tripling of pension expenditure as share of output.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexican government","action":"increased pension spending","mechanism":["demographic aging","reform-driven spending expansion"],"outcome":"Pension spending nearly tripled as share of GDP from 1.4% to 4.0% over two decades","dates":["2000","2021"],"quantities":["1.4 percent of GDP","4.0 percent of GDP"],"excerpt":"government spending on pensions already increased from 1.4 percent of GDP in 2000 to 4.0
percent of GDP in 2021","locator":"page 92","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"2000-2021 trajectory","source_limitations":["Historical baseline from 2000; does not yet reflect 2020/2021 reform spending impacts","4.0% GDP spending level will rise further in near term as reforms take effect"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 92. Quantities (1.4%, 4.0%) and dates (2000, 2021) match source. The 'near-tripling' characterization is a reasonable inference from the stated figures. Attribution is correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0168","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The pension reforms may adversely affect labor market incentives by enabling early retirement (reducing labor force participation among older workers), reducing incentives to remain in formal employment except near earnings or career length thresholds, and increasing the employer contribution rate which may push workers into the informal sector.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"IMF staff","action":"identified adverse labor market effects from pension reform","mechanism":["early retirement option reducing labor force participation","minimum pension linked to earnings history reducing formal employment incentives near thresholds","employer contribution rate increase increasing labor wedge","government subsidies for low earners partially offsetting informality incentive"],"outcome":"Tangible decline in labor force participation among older workers possible; increased informality risk despite formal participation incentives","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"By
enabling early retirement, the reforms could result in a tangible decline in labor force participation
amongst older workers. Moreover, the linking of the minimum pension to earnings history may
reduce incentives to remain in (formal) employment except for those who are close to one of the
earnings or career length thresholds. Finally, the increase in the contribution rate for employers may
serve to increase the labor wedge, impacting employment and pushing more workers into the
already large informal sector despite incentives for formal participation as a result of the
government's efforts to subsidize pension contributions for low earners","locator":"page 92","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"Medium-term labor market effects as of 2022 assessment","source_limitations":["These are forward-looking adverse effect identifications, not confirmed realized outcomes","Government subsidies for low earners partially offset the informality push","Phased implementation may mitigate some labor market disruptions"],"question_ids":["5B.8"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 92. The claim accurately synthesizes the three labor market concerns from the source. Attribution to IMF is correct. Polarity and claim_type are appropriate for a forward-looking staff identification of adverse effects."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0169","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's exports to Central America constitute 1.7 percent of total exports and imports from Central America comprise 0.6 percent of total imports in 2021, indicating surprisingly low bilateral trade despite geographical proximity and a regional free trade agreement.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexico","action":"traded with Central America","mechanism":["geographical proximity","regional free trade agreement (2011/2013)"],"outcome":"Low trade intensity: 1.7% of Mexican exports to Central America; 0.6% of Mexican imports from Central America","dates":["2021"],"quantities":["1.7 percent of total exports","0.6 percent of total imports"],"excerpt":"Mexico's exports to Central America
constitute a mere 1.7 percent of its total exports in 2021, while the country's imports from Central
America comprise 0.6 percent of total imports","locator":"page 93","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; source data from United Nations Comtrade Database","period_fit":"2021","source_limitations":["Data sourced from UN Comtrade; 2021 data used where 2021 not yet available","Low trade figures could reflect supply chain, competitiveness, or policy barriers not identified in this passage"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.10"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 93. The source uses 'a mere 1.7 percent' while the claim uses '1.7 percent' - the claim correctly omits the editorial qualifier. Quantities (1.7%, 0.6%) and date (2021) match source. Attribution to IMF Article IV with UN Comtrade as underlying data source is correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0170","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Central America's exposure to Mexico comprises approximately 5.8 percent of the region's total exports going to Mexico and 13.5 percent of imports coming from Mexico in 2021, with Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Belize having the highest export exposure (over 8 percent to Mexico) and Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras having the highest import exposure (over 15 percent from Mexico).","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Central American countries","action":"traded with Mexico","mechanism":["Mexico-Central America free trade agreement (2011/2013)"],"outcome":"Asymmetric regional trade exposure: exports to Mexico lower than imports from Mexico; Nicaragua's export exposure increased substantially after FTA implementation","dates":["2021"],"quantities":["5.8 percent of region's exports","13.5 percent of imports","8 percent","15 percent"],"excerpt":"Central America's exposure to Mexico,
though has increased over time, is low with around 5.8 percent of the region's total exports going to
Mexico in 2021 and 13.5 percent of the imports coming from Mexico","locator":"page 93","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; source data from United Nations Comtrade Database","period_fit":"2021","source_limitations":["Nicaragua's export exposure increase post-FTA is noted but other countries' responses to FTA are not individually quantified","2020 data used where 2021 not yet available from Comtrade"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.10"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 93. The additional country-level details (Nicaragua, Guatemala, Belize for exports over 8%; Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras for imports over 15%) are also present in the source text. Attribution to IMF with UN Comtrade as underlying source is correct. The source notes that 2020 data is used where 2021 is not yet available."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0171","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico and Central American countries could gain substantial benefits to growth from further trade integration as there is a close match between the top products exported by Mexico and those imported by Central America, with machinery and equipment being Mexico's second-most exported and Central America's second-most imported product.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"IMF staff","action":"identified trade integration growth potential","mechanism":["product complementarity between Mexico's exports and Central America's imports","machinery and equipment trade match"],"outcome":"Substantial potential growth gains from inter- and intra-regional trade integration","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Mexico and its Central American neighbors could gain substantial benefits to growth from further trade integration as there is potential to increase both inter- and intra-regional trade. Given the close match between the top products exported by Mexico and those imported by Central America (e.g., machinery and equipment is Mexico's second-most exported and Central America's second-most imported product), there is scope for Mexico to increase exports to this region","locator":"page 93","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report (citing IMF 2017)","period_fit":"Current/recent as of 2022","source_limitations":["Trade integration gains are projected/potential rather than realized","Implementation barriers (customs, infrastructure, nontariff barriers) not quantified in this passage"],"question_ids":["5B.4","5B.10"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 93. Attribution includes the citation to IMF 2017 as in the source text. Polarity (favorable) correctly reflects the beneficial nature of the staff assessment. Claim type and question mapping are appropriate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0172","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's overall nontariff trade restrictions are around the middle range compared to Central American countries, with some Central American countries remaining at high restriction levels for many years, indicating uneven trade policy liberalization under the free trade agreement.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexico and Central American governments","action":"maintained varying levels of nontariff trade restrictions","mechanism":["nontariff barriers measured as official government policy toward international goods and services flow (excluding tariffs)","data from IMF Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions"],"outcome":"Mexico mid-range on nontariff restrictions; some Central American countries persistently high; reducing barriers from both sides would facilitate further regional integration","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Mexico's overall nontariff trade
restrictions is around the middle range. Some Central American countries have remained flat at high
restriction levels for many years","locator":"page 94","attribution":"International Monetary Fund (source: Estefania-Flores et. al 2022, IMF Working Paper WP/22/1; IMF Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions)","period_fit":"Cross-sectional measure as of 2022 data","source_limitations":["Nontariff barrier measure is aggregate; specific product-level or sector-level barriers not disclosed","Some Central American countries' persistently high restrictions may reflect domestic policy constraints beyond trade negotiations"],"question_ids":["5B.4"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 94. The mechanism detail about nontariff barrier measurement methodology is consistent with the source note. Attribution to the Estefania-Flores et al. 2022 IMF Working Paper and IMF Annual Report on Exchange Arrangements and Exchange Restrictions is appropriate. Polarity (mixed) correctly captures both Mexico's middle-range position and some Central American countries' persistently high levels."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0173","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Reducing nontariff trade barriers from both Mexico and Central American countries would facilitate further integration, with strengthened customs cooperation potentially going a long way, including replicating at the Southern border the cooperation programs and mechanisms in place with the United States following the 1994 NAFTA.","claim_type":"recommendation","polarity":"favorable","actor":"IMF staff","action":"recommended trade facilitation measures","mechanism":["reducing nontariff barriers bilaterally","customs cooperation replication from US-Mexico border cooperation","border infrastructure improvement","capacity development and risk management","bottleneck reduction"],"outcome":"Improved trade coordination, infrastructure, and capacity at Mexico's Southern border","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Strengthened customs cooperation could go a long way in facilitating Mexico's trade
with this region. Mexico could replicate in the Southern border the cooperation programs and
mechanisms in place with the U.S. following the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement","locator":"page 95","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report (citing IMF 2022)","period_fit":"Prospective policy recommendation as of 2022","source_limitations":["This is a policy recommendation, not an implemented reform","Replication of US border cooperation at Southern border would require significant institutional and security coordination","Migrant and security policy dimensions at Southern border add complexity beyond trade facilitation"],"question_ids":["5B.4"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 95. Claim type correctly identifies this as a recommendation. The candidate accurately separates the customs cooperation recommendation from the broader 'reducing nontariff trade barriers' context, both of which appear in the source. The NAFTA/1994 citation is correctly attributed to IMF 2022 within the source document. Attribution is appropriate."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0174","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Data provision is adequate for surveillance; Mexico's national accounts follow the 2008 SNA and were found to be of high quality by the 2021 Data ROSC update, with significant improvements made in methodological and dissemination aspects since 2015.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"INEGI (National Statistical Office of Mexico)","action":"produced and disseminated economic statistics","mechanism":["2008 SNA compliance","five-year economic censuses","monthly and annual surveys","administrative data","business register of economic units"],"outcome":"High-quality national accounts meeting international surveillance standards","dates":["2021 (Data ROSC update)","2015 (significant methodological improvements)"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Data provision is adequate for surveillance. The national accounts follow the recommendations of the System of National Accounts, 2008 (2008 SNA). The 2021 data ROSC update found that the national accounts are of a high quality.","locator":"page 100","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; Data ROSC December 2021","period_fit":"Current data quality assessment as of 2022 Article IV consultation","source_limitations":["Areas for further improvement remain: chained GDP volume indices, treatment of goods for processing abroad, coverage of illegal activities, quarterly government transactions recorded on cash rather than accrual basis","Reconciliation between Banxico, SHCP, and INEGI data remains needed","Some areas for improvement are not yet implemented"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 100. The mechanism elements (2008 SNA, economic censuses, surveys, administrative data, business register) are consistent with the source text description. Actor (INEGI) is appropriate as the producing agency. Attribution to IMF Article IV and Data ROSC December 2021 is correct. The source limitations are consistent with additional source text on page 100."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0175","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Both the CPI and PPI meet international standards for concepts and definitions; CPI basket is based on National Survey of Household Expenditure 2012-2013, 2014 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, and 1999 COICOP classification; PPI covers 79.2 percent of Mexican production excluding trade and some services.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"INEGI","action":"compiled price indices","mechanism":["National Survey of Household Expenditure","Household Income and Expenditure Survey","COICOP classification","Economic Censuses and System of National Accounts"],"outcome":"CPI and PPI meet international standards; CPI reference period: second half of July 2018; PPI reference period: July 2019","dates":["2012","2013","2014","2019"],"quantities":["79.2 percent of Mexican production"],"excerpt":"The concepts and definitions for both the CPI and PPI meet international standards.
The CPI reference period is the second half of July 2018, and the basket is based on
information from the National Survey of Household Expenditure 2012 and 2013, the 2014
Household Income and Expenditure Survey, and the 1999 COICOP classification","locator":"page 100","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; Data ROSC December 2021","period_fit":"Current as of 2022 consultation","source_limitations":["CPI basket based on 2012-2014 survey data may not fully reflect current consumption patterns","PPI excludes trade and some services sectors"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 100. The PPI coverage detail (79.2% of Mexican production excluding trade and some services) and PPI reference period (July 2019) are present in the source text. Attribution to IMF Article IV and Data ROSC December 2021 is correct. Quantities (79.2%) and dates match source."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0176","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Fiscal statistics are comprehensive and timely except for the subnational sector; Mexico compiles fiscal statistics following both domestic concepts and GFSM2014, though differences in classification and institutional unit coverage make reconciliation difficult; pension liabilities are partially reported and official debt statistics exclude T-bonds issued to Banxico for liquidity management.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican authorities (Ministry of Finance / SHCP)","action":"compiled and reported fiscal statistics","mechanism":["domestic fiscal compilation","GFSM2014 alignment","partial pension liability reporting","face value reporting of government securities"],"outcome":"Comprehensive central government fiscal data; subnational data gaps; reconciliation difficulties between domestic and international presentations; incomplete pension and certain debt reporting","dates":[],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Fiscal statistics are comprehensive and timely, except for the subnational sector. The authorities compile fiscal statistics following national concepts, definitions, and classifications to support domestic policy needs. The authorities also compile fiscal statistics in alignment with the Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM2014). Pension liabilities are partially reported, while government securities are reported at face value.","locator":"page 100","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; Data ROSC 2021","period_fit":"Current as of 2022","source_limitations":["Subnational fiscal data gap limits comprehensive fiscal surveillance","Debt statistics exclude certain instruments (T-bonds for liquidity management); accounting practices with Banxico differ","These are identified data quality limitations that affect fiscal transparency"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 100. The T-bond exclusion detail is present in the source text on page 101. Attribution to IMF Article IV and Data ROSC 2021 is correct. The claim accurately synthesizes the fiscal statistics quality issues from the source. Polarity (mixed) is appropriate for a mix of comprehensive/positive aspects and identified limitations."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0177","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico regularly reports monthly Financial Soundness Indicators (FSIs) to the IMF for publication, currently reporting 14 core and 9 encouraged indicators for deposit takers plus additional indicators for OFCs, households, and real estate markets, though reporting was temporarily interrupted after May 2021 for IFRS9 standards revision.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican authorities (Banxico)","action":"reported Financial Soundness Indicators","mechanism":["monthly FSI reporting to IMF","IFRS9 standards revision"],"outcome":"14 core and 9 encouraged FSI indicators for deposit takers; 2 additional for OFCs; 1 for households; 1 for real estate markets; reporting temporarily interrupted for standards update","dates":["May 2021"],"quantities":["14 core indicators","9 encouraged indicators","2 additional (OFCs)","1 (households)","1 (real estate markets)"],"excerpt":"Mexico regularly reports monthly Financial Soundness
Indicators (FSIs) to the IMF for publication. Currently, Mexico reports 14 core and 9
encouraged indicators for deposit takers, 2 additional FSI for OFCs,1 additional FSI for
households and 1 additional FSI for real estate markets","locator":"page 101","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"Current as of 2022; reporting interrupted from May 2021 pending IFRS9 revision","source_limitations":["FSI reporting for non-financial corporate sector not reported","Temporary reporting interruption pending IFRS9 revision (as of 2022 assessment)","Real estate market FSI only 1 indicator vs. broader scope for other sectors"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 101. The source notes reporting was temporarily interrupted following publication of May 2021 data for IFRS9 revision. The candidate includes this qualification. Quantities (14 core, 9 encouraged, 2 OFCs, 1 household, 1 real estate) match source. Attribution is correct."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0178","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"External sector statistics were found to be of high quality by the 2021 Data ROSC update; Banxico migrated BOP and IIP statistics to BPM6 in 2017; remaining issues include intercompany external debt, market valuation of liabilities, and accrual basis recording of public sector external debt interest.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Banxico","action":"produced and reported external sector statistics","mechanism":["BPM6 migration in 2017","coordinated direct investment survey","coordinated portfolio investment survey"],"outcome":"High-quality external sector statistics per 2021 Data ROSC; quarterly BPM6-based BOP and IIP data published; but consistency between IIP and external debt needs improvement; some financial account and position discrepancies with national accounts","dates":["2017","2021"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The 2021 data ROSC update found that ESS are of a high
quality. In 2017, Banxico migrated the BOP and IIP statistics to the Balance of Payments and
International Investment Position Manual (BPM6), sixth edition","locator":"page 101","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report; Data ROSC December 2021","period_fit":"Current as of 2022","source_limitations":["External Debt Statistics Guide (2013) not yet fully implemented","Intercompany external debt and SDR allocations not yet included in external debt statistics","Some external debt presented at face value rather than market value","Public sector external debt interest not yet recorded on accrual basis","IIP and external debt consistency gaps remain","Balance of payments and national accounts discrepancies in financial account"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 101. The remaining issues (intercompany debt, market valuation, accrual recording of interest) are enumerated in the source text. Attribution to IMF Article IV and Data ROSC December 2021 is correct. Dates (2017, 2021) and mechanism elements are consistent with source. The source notes SDS Guide 2013 not yet fully implemented as an additional limitation."],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0179","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico subscribed to the IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) on August 13, 1996, and the latest SDDS Observance Report and metadata are available on the Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board; Mexico uses SDDS flexibility options on central government debt and general government operations and exceeds SDDS requirements in many categories.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexico","action":"subscribed to IMF SDDS","mechanism":["SDDS subscription and compliance","periodicity and timeliness flexibility options"],"outcome":"SDDS subscriber since 1996; exceeds SDDS requirements in many data categories; updated Data ROSC published December 2021","dates":["August 13, 1996","December 2021"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Mexico subscribed to the IMF's Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) on August 13, 1996. Mexico exceeds SDDS periodicity and timeliness requirements in many other data categories.","locator":"page 102","attribution":"International Monetary Fund, Mexico Article IV Consultation Report","period_fit":"SDDS subscription since 1996; current compliance as of 2022","source_limitations":["This is a data standards and metadata statement; it describes institutional commitment rather than policy outcomes","Use of flexibility options on central government debt and general government operations means some categories do not meet full SDDS standard"],"question_ids":["5B.7"],"verification_status":"accepted","verification_notes":["Excerpt verified verbatim in source text page 102. The SDDS subscription date (August 13, 1996) and the statement about exceeding SDDS periodicity and timeliness requirements are verbatim matches. The flexibility options detail is also present in the source table on page 102. Attribution is correct. Date (December 2021) for updated Data ROSC is present in the source."],"premium_verification_required":false}],"material_omissions":[],"unresolved_gaps":[]}
